Synthesis:
The Federal Aviation Administration records National Airspace System delays in the OPSNET database for instrument flight rules traffic delayed by 15 minutes or more [1][2]. Reports categorize these delays by cause: Weather, Volume, Equipment, Runway, and Other [3][1]. In 2024, there were 359,694 total reportable delays totaling 16,065,315 minutes [2]. Staffing shortages are tracked as a subcategory of Other and accounted for 12,711 delays and 622,669 minutes in 2024 [2]. Data for these metrics are accessible via the FAA???s ASPM website using the Delay By Cause or Standard reports [3][4][5].

Jump to: navigation, search

In OPSNET Delays, the Standard Report displays the total number of System Impact Delays per selected grouping variable. The user can choose to display the data by date, facility, state, region, service area, and user class. The only two required selections to run a standard report are Data and Grouping.

Clicking on the highlighted values in the 'TMI To', 'TMI From', 'Airborne', and 'Airborne Destination To Delays', will display a pop-up window with the list of facilities the delayed aircraft were going to or coming from.

For information about how to create a Standard Report, see the OPSNET Manual.

## D Estimating the Cost of Staffing-Related Flight Delays

This appendix draws on Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) data on delays, including those attributed to staffing, to estimate the cost of these staffing-related delays. All data are drawn from FAA???s Operations Network (OPSNET) database. After reviewing trends in delays, an estimate is made of their costs to passengers and airlines.

The estimated cost of delays in 2024 caused by FAA Air Traffic Control (ATC) staffing shortfalls ranges between $135 million and $165 million, although, as noted below, this estimate does not include delay-related costs the committee is unable to account for due to data inadequacies.

### FAA DELAY DATA

FAA provides information about delays reported daily through FAA???s OPSNET. A reportable delay is defined as ???delays to instrument flight rules (IFR) traffic of 15 minutes or more, which result from the ATC system detaining an aircraft at the gate, short of the runway, on the runway, on a taxiway, or in a holding configuration anywhere en route.??? The delays are then classified into five primary causes:

1. Weather: adverse weather conditions affecting operations.
2. Volume: delays due to volume when airport is in optimal configuration with no impacting conditions.
3. Runway: Reductions in capacity due to runway/taxiway closure or configuration changes.

Page 244

Bookmark

Suggested Citation: "Appendix D: Estimating the Cost of Staffing-Related Flight Delays." National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. 2025. The Air Traffic Controller Workforce Imperative: Staffing Models and Their Implementation to Ensure Safe and Efficient Airspace Operations. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press. doi: 10.17226/29112.

Save

Cancel

1. Equipment: ATC equipment failure or outage causing reduced capacity.
2. Other: All impacting conditions not elsewhere classified, such as airshows, VIP restrictions, military operations. Staffing shortfalls were added as subcategory of ???Other Delays??? beginning in mid-2022.

Table D-1 shows delays by cause for calendar years 2015???2024, as well as averages for 2015???2019 (pre-COVID), 2020???2021 (COVID), 2022???2024 (post-COVID). Reductions in weather-related delays account for most of the decline in total delays. Runway and volume delays have declined slightly, while delays due to equipment have risen in numbers and duration. The number of delays attributed to ???Other Factors??? (including staffing) has been more variable, including an unprecedented decrease in 2023 relative to 2022 and 2024 (as well as to pre-COVID years). The committee was not able to identify any reporting changes that would explain the 2023 anomaly. Because of this variability, it used the average of the 2022???2024 period. The average duration of Other Delays has increased from 30 minutes in 2015???2019 to 45 minutes in 2022???2024. All the delay metrics in Table D-1 increased dramatically in 2024 compared to a year earlier.

As staffing delays are subsumed within the Other Delays category, we reviewed the longer-term mix of Other Delays, as shown in Table D-2.

Table D-2 shows that from 2015 to 2019 the share of Other Delays (which includes staffing) were relatively stable, averaging about 5.0% of delays and 3.3% of delay minutes. For the overall 2022???2024 period, there is a marked rise in Other Delays to 6.1% of delays and 6.7% of delay-minutes.

### DISTRIBUTION OF TOTAL AND OTHER DELAYS JANUARY 2022???DECEMBER 2024

Table D-3 shows that the Other Delays category was concentrated in the Core 30 Airport facilities (Towers, TRACONS, Tower and Approach Control, and Centers) as well as in the 19 facilities defined as ???staffing levels 15% below their standard??? in Chapter 2. These 19 facilities (1 Level 9, 18 Levels 10???12) represent approximately 22% of operations, but about 40% of Total Delays and about 45% of Other Delays (which include staffing-related delays).

### DELAYS BY SECONDARY CAUSE

Beginning in June 2022, FAA added a new secondary subcategory to the ???Other Delays??? category. This classification occurs when a facility reports delays due to insufficient staffing. The data are reported in terms of the number of flights delayed, as well as the duration of each delay. Thus, to estimate the total delay due to staffing, it is necessary to aggregate all the flights and the associated time they were affected by the staffing delay. The results are shown in Table D-4. The table shows that delays due to staffing shortages have grown rapidly and now represent more than half of Other Delays. In 2024, the 12,711 delays due to staffing represented 622,669 minutes of delay, averaging 49 minutes.

As shown in Table D-5, of the 622,669 minutes of staffing-related aircraft delays, 86% were attributed to just seven facilities.

Synthesis:
The FAA does not publish a pre-calculated, static ranking report for 2024 ARTCC delay minutes [1][2]. You can generate this data by accessing the Aviation System Performance Metrics (ASPM) OPSNET Delays interface [1][3]. Use the Ranking Report feature to select ZNY, ZDC, and ZAU as your facilities and specify the date range for 2024 [1]. The system will then provide the total minutes and average delay metrics for those centers [1][4]. Raw data can also be exported via the Summary Data Download tool for custom analysis [4][5].

<url>https://aspmhelp.faa.gov/index/OPSNET__Delays.html</url>
<content>OPSNET Delays provides information about reportable delays provided daily through FAA's Air Traffic Operations Network (OPSNET). A reportable delay recorded in OPSNET is defined in FAA Order 7210.55F as, "Delays to instrument flight rules (IFR) traffic of 15 minutes or more, which result from the ATC system detaining an aircraft at the gate, short of the runway, on the runway, on a taxiway, or in a holding configuration anywhere en route, must be reported. The IFR controlling facility must ensure delay reports are received and entered into OPSNET." These OPSNET delays are caused by the application of initiatives by the Traffic Flow Management (TFM) in response to weather conditions, increased traffic volume, runway conditions, equipment outages, and other causes.
...
The Standard, Comparison, Ranking, and Peak Days reports in OPSNET show both System Impact Delay, in which delay is attributed to the causal facility, and Occurred at Delay, which shows the amount of delay experienced by operations at each facility. The other OPSNET reports attribute delays to the causal facility only (System Impact).</content>

Synthesis:
The Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) tracks flight delays using five categories: Air Carrier, National Aviation System (NAS), Weather, Late-Arriving Aircraft, and Security [1][2]. A flight is considered delayed if it arrives 15 or more minutes behind schedule [3][4].

NAS delays include non-extreme weather, airport operations, heavy traffic, and air traffic control [1][2]. Because airlines do not report causes for late-arriving aircraft, the BTS prorates these delays based on the distribution of other reported categories to estimate the true impact of factors like weather [1][5].

Highlights:
<result id="1">
<title>Understanding the Reporting of Causes of Flight Delays and Cancellations | Bureau of Transportation Statistics</title>
<url>https://www.bts.gov/topics/airlines-and-airports/understanding-reporting-causes-flight-delays-and-cancellations</url>
<content>The airlines report the
...
delay in broad
...
Time Reporting Advisory
...
System, Weather,
...
Is it true that weather causes only 4 percent of flight delays? That category consists of extreme weather that prevents flying. There is another category of weather within the NAS category. This type of weather slows the operations of the system but does not prevent flying. Delays or cancellations coded "NAS" are the type of weather delays that could be reduced with corrective action by the airports or the Federal Aviation Administration. During 2020, 45.8% of NAS delays were due to weather. NAS delays were 33.4% of total delays in 2020.
...
How many flights were really delayed by weather? A true picture of total weather-related delays requires several steps. First, the extreme weather delays must be combined with the NAS weather category. Second, a calculation must be made to determine the weather-related delays included in the "late-arriving aircraft" category. Airlines do not report the causes of the late-arriving aircraft but an allocation can be made using the proportion of weather related-delays and total flights in the other categories. Adding the weather-related delays to the extreme weather and NAS weather categories would result in weather's share of all flight delays.
...
Is more information available on the causes of delays and cancellations? Cause of delay numbers can be found on the BTS website at http://www.transtats.bts.gov/OT_Delay/OT_DelayCause1.asp This page allows searches by time period and by airline or airport. It also has calculations for weather???s share of flight delays and a breakdown of NAS delays by category. More data can be found on the TranStats database. Also, the Department???s monthly Air Travel Consumer Report includes a summary of causes of delay numbers reported by each carrier for the most recent month. The report can be found at http://www.dot.gov/airconsumer/air-travel-consumer-reports.</content>
</result>

<result id="2">
<title>Airline On-Time Performance and Causes of Flight Delays | Bureau of Transportation Statistics</title>
<url>https://www.bts.gov/explore-topics-and-geography/topics/airline-time-performance-and-causes-flight-delays</url>
<content>Which operating carriers report on-time performance, causes of flight delays causes of flight delays, tarmac times, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs/scooters and denied boardings? Carriers that have 0.5 percent of total domestic scheduled-service passenger revenue report on-time data and the causes of delay. In 2021, there are 17 carriers required to report these numbers. The reports cover nonstop scheduled-service flights between points within the United States (including territories) as described in 14 CFR Part 234 of DOT's regulations.
...
What types of flight delays are reported to BTS by the airlines? Airlines that report monthly numbers of flight delays to the BTS began reporting information on causes of delays in June 2003. The airlines report the causes of delays in five broad categories:
...
- Air Carrier: The cause of the cancellation or delay was due to circumstances within the airline's control (e.g. maintenance or crew problems, aircraft cleaning, baggage loading, fueling, etc.).
...
- Extreme Weather: Significant meteorological conditions (actual or forecasted) that, in the judgment of the carrier, delays or prevents the operation of a flight such as tornado, blizzard or hurricane.
...
- National Aviation System (NAS): Delays and cancellations attributable to the national aviation system that refer to a broad set of conditions, such as non-extreme weather conditions, airport operations, heavy traffic volume, and air traffic control.
...
A flight is counted as "on time" if it operated less than 15 minutes later than the scheduled time shown in the carriers' Computerized Reservations Systems (CRS). Arrival performance is based on arrival at the gate. Departure performance is based on departure from the gate.
...
What types of data are published? The U.S. Department of Transportation publishes a monthly summary of airline on-time performance, including causes of delay, in the Air Travel Consumer Report.</content>

                      tickFormatter={(v) =>

                      domain={metric === "share" ? [0, 100] : ["auto", "auto"]}

                      formatter={(value, name) => {

                            fmtPct(n),
                            CAUSE_META[name as CauseId]?.label ?? name,

                          CAUSE_META[name as CauseId]?.label ?? name,

                        stackId="1"

                        fillOpacity={0.85}
                      />

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

export type ThemeBalanceRow = {
  themeId: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  count: number;
  sharePct: number;
  consecutive: number;
  overCap: boolean;
  underTarget: boolean;
};

export function getThemeById(id: string): ThemeDefinition | undefined {
  return THEME_REGISTRY.find((t) => t.id === id && t.status === "active");
}

export function resolveThemeId(slug: string, themeId?: string): string | undefined {
  if (themeId) return themeId;
  return SLUG_THEME_IDS[slug];
}

export function computeThemeBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): ThemeBalanceRow[] {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    counts.set(tid, (counts.get(tid) ?? 0) + 1);
  }

  const consecutiveByTheme = new Map<string, number>();
  let lastTheme: string | undefined;
  let streak = 0;
  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) break;
    if (tid === lastTheme) streak++;
    else {
      lastTheme = tid;
      streak = 1;
    }
    consecutiveByTheme.set(tid, streak);
  }

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((t) => t.status === "active").map((theme) => {
    const count = counts.get(theme.id) ?? 0;
    const sharePct = (count / total) * 100;
    return {
      themeId: theme.id,
      label: theme.label,
      lane: theme.lane,
      count,
      sharePct,
      consecutive: consecutiveByTheme.get(theme.id) ?? 0,
      overCap: sharePct > theme.maxSharePct,
      underTarget: sharePct < theme.targetSharePct * 0.5 && count === 0,
    };
  });
}

export function computeLaneBalance(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
  window = BALANCE_CONFIG.rollingWindow,
): Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }> {
  const recent = slugThemePairs.slice(0, window);
  const total = recent.length || 1;
  const lanes = Object.keys(LANE_LABELS) as ThemeLane[];
  const out = {} as Record<ThemeLane, { count: number; sharePct: number }>;

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane] = { count: 0, sharePct: 0 };
  }

  for (const post of recent) {
    const tid = resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId);
    if (!tid) continue;
    const theme = getThemeById(tid);
    if (!theme) continue;
    out[theme.lane].count++;
  }

  for (const lane of lanes) {
    out[lane].sharePct = (out[lane].count / total) * 100;
  }

  return out;
}

/** Pick themes eligible for next post (not over cap, not over consecutive) */
export function getEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): ThemeDefinition[] {
  const balance = computeThemeBalance(slugThemePairs);
  const laneBalance = computeLaneBalance(slugThemePairs);

  const recentLane =
    slugThemePairs.length > 0
      ? getThemeById(resolveThemeId(slugThemePairs[0].slug, slugThemePairs[0].themeId) ?? "")?.lane
      : undefined;

  let consecutiveLane = 0;
  if (recentLane) {
    for (const post of slugThemePairs) {
      const lane = getThemeById(resolveThemeId(post.slug, post.themeId) ?? "")?.lane;
      if (lane === recentLane) consecutiveLane++;
      else break;
    }
  }

  const overCapLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct > BALANCE_CONFIG.laneHardCapPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  const starvedLanes = (Object.entries(laneBalance) as [ThemeLane, { sharePct: number }][])
    .filter(([, v]) => v.sharePct < BALANCE_CONFIG.laneStarvationPct)
    .map(([k]) => k);

  return THEME_REGISTRY.filter((theme) => {
    if (theme.status !== "active") return false;
    const row = balance.find((b) => b.themeId === theme.id);
    if (row?.overCap) return false;
    if ((row?.consecutive ?? 0) >= theme.maxConsecutive) return false;
    if (overCapLanes.includes(theme.lane)) return false;
    if (consecutiveLane >= BALANCE_CONFIG.maxConsecutivePerLane && theme.lane === recentLane) {
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }).sort((a, b) => {
    const aStarved = starvedLanes.includes(a.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    const bStarved = starvedLanes.includes(b.lane) ? 1 : 0;
    if (aStarved !== bStarved) return bStarved - aStarved;
    const aCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === a.id)?.count ?? 0;
    const bCount = balance.find((r) => r.themeId === b.id)?.count ?? 0;
    return aCount - bCount;
  });
}

export function getBacklogFromEligibleThemes(
  slugThemePairs: Array<{ slug: string; themeId?: string }>,
): Array<PipelineCandidate & { themeId: string; themeLabel: string }> {
  const eligible = getEligibleThemes(slugThemePairs);
  return eligible.flatMap((theme) =>
    theme.candidates.map((c) => ({
      ...c,
      themeId: theme.id,
      themeLabel: theme.label,
      title: `[${theme.label}] ${c.title}`,
    })),
  );
}

/** Criteria for agent-proposed new themes ??? append to THEME_REGISTRY when all pass */
export type NewThemeProposal = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  lane: ThemeLane;
  category: Category;
  metaQuestion: string;
  visualLane: string;
  targetSharePct: number;
  maxSharePct: number;
  maxConsecutive: number;
  candidates: PipelineCandidate[];
  justification: string;
};

export function validateNewThemeProposal(proposal: NewThemeProposal): string[] {
  const errors: string[] = [];
  if (!/^[a-z0-9-]+$/.test(proposal.id)) errors.push("id must be kebab-case");
  if (THEME_REGISTRY.some((t) => t.id === proposal.id)) errors.push("id already exists");
  if (proposal.candidates.length < 2) errors.push("need ???2 seed candidates");
  if (proposal.targetSharePct < 4 || proposal.targetSharePct > 15) {
    errors.push("targetSharePct should be 4???15");
  }
  if (!proposal.justification || proposal.justification.length < 40) {
    errors.push("justification too short");
  }
  return errors;
}

import type { Post } from "@/types/post";

export const samplePosts: Post[] = [
  {
    id: "measurement-science-geography-2026",
    slug: "measurement-science-geography-2026",
    title:
      "Charted: China Holds 29.4% of World GERD ??? East Asia ~41%; Pubs and Patents Tip Harder",
    excerpt:
      "Geography lens on measurement & science: China 29.4% / US 29.1% of ~$3.48T PPP GERD, East Asia ~41% of funding, China 31% of S&E pubs and ~75% of CET AI priority patents ??? while KTI value-added still crowns the US at 28%.",
    category: "Global Systems",
    themeId: "measurement-science",
    imageUrl:
      "/images/global-systems-measurement-science-geography-2026-hero.png",
    imageAlt:
      "Dark navy cinematic data-viz of a glowing world map with amber East Asia R&D bars, cyan North America knife-edge stacks, and violet patent arcs",
    publishedAt: "2026-08-21T23:45:00Z",
    featured: true,
    visualization: "measurement-science-geography-2026",
    layout: "default",
    content: `Our theme already maps *who* funds and publishes science at the top of the distribution. The [2026 concentration print](/blog/measurement-science-concentration-2026) scored GERD PPP Top-1 / Top-3. The [Q3 concentration restatement](/blog/measurement-science-concentration-2026q3) carried the knife-edge. The [August 202608 concentration companion](/blog/measurement-science-concentration-202608) then asked whether China???s 2025 domestic ?? flow and CET patent meters change tip geometry without splicing yuan into PPP shares. This post answers the map question desks trade next: **where does R&D funding, publication volume, and patent activity sit geographically ??? and do those maps agree?**

The interactive dashboard above is built as a **geography lens**, not another Top-k ladder. Toggle **Countries**, **Regions**, **Share paths**, and **Funding vs output**. The punchline is deliberately multi-map. On *GERD PPP funding*, **China holds about 29.4%** of a ~**$3.48T** world ??? a **0.3 pp** knife-edge over the United States at **29.1%**. On *regional blocs*, **East Asia clears about 41%** of world GERD. On *S&E publication volume*, China tips harder at **31%** while the US falls to **12%** and India enters Top-3 at **7%**. On *CET AI priority patents*, China jumps to about **75%**. On *KTI value-added*, the **United States still leads at 28%**. Same theme, five different geographic tips.

## The geography scoreboard

| Lens | Top-1 share | Top-1 tip | What it measures |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| GERD funding (PPP) | **29.4%** | China | OECD/AAAS 2024 world ~$3.48T |
| East Asia GERD bloc | **~41%** | E. Asia | China + Japan + Korea roll-up |
| S&E publication volume | **31%** | China | NSF Indicators 2024 fractional |
| CET AI priority patents | **~75%** | China | NSF Translation field tip |
| KTI value-added | **28%** | United States | World KTI VA ~$11.7T |
| USPTO utility applicants | **~47%** | United States | Domestic utility grant geography |

Read the table as a **family of maps**, not one slogan. Funding geography says China and the US are co-dominant at the country tip, with East Asia the thickest *bloc*. Publication geography says China already leads by a wide margin and India punches into Top-3. Patent geography splits: CET critical-and-emerging fields tip hard to China; USPTO utility applicants still tip to the US. KTI value-added geography puts the US first even while China leads manufacturing VA inside the same perimeter. Averaging these rows into ???science has moved to China??? is true on pubs and CET patents and false on KTI VA and USPTO utility.

## Countries: Tip-1 relocates when you change the perimeter

Open **Countries**. On GERD PPP, China **29.4%** and the US **29.1%** sit within rounding of each other; Japan **6.7%**, Germany **5.5%**, and Korea **4.7%** fill the next rungs; Top-3 (China + US + Japan) clears about **65%**. Flip the perimeter to **Publications** and China rises to **31%** while the US drops to **12%** and India appears at **7%** ??? Top-3 becomes China + US + India at **50%**. Flip again to **CET AI patents** and China alone is about **75%**. Flip to **KTI VA** and the US reclaims Tip-1 at **28%**, with China **25%** and EU-27 **18%**. Flip to **USPTO utility** and the US leads at about **47%**.

That relocation is the operational hinge. Desks that underwrite ???China won science??? from publication volume are reading one map. Desks that underwrite knowledge-and-technology *industry* value-added are reading another. Desks that underwrite USPTO utility grants are reading a third. The [August concentration companion](/blog/measurement-science-concentration-202608) already showed tip disagreement across perimeters; geography makes the disagreement *spatial*.

## Regions: East Asia owns the funding bloc; North America still owns KTI Tip-1

Toggle **Regions**. On GERD PPP, **East Asia holds about 41%** of world funding (~**$1.42T** of the **$3.48T** perimeter). North America is about **32%**, Europe about **18%**, South Asia about **2%**, and the residual closes the rest. Flip to publications and East Asia stays thick (~**36%**) while South Asia???s India tip lifts that bloc???s share; North America???s *share* collapses relative to its funding weight because US publication volume did not keep pace with US GERD share. Flip to CET AI patents and East Asia jumps toward **~80%** ??? the regional expression of China???s ~**75%** country tip.

Inside the US funding tip, state geography still densifies. California alone is about **22%** of US domestic R&D on the desk roll-up; Massachusetts, Texas, New York, and Washington fill the next band. Flip the US-state metric to **Intensity %** and Massachusetts leads; flip to **Dollars** and California???s absolute stack dominates. World GERD geography and *inside-US* R&D geography are nested maps ??? do not confuse a California campus story with a China/US knife-edge.

## Share paths: the knife-edge was earned over a decade

    slug: "us-atc-delay-minutes-by-cause-2026",
    title:
      "Charted: Weather Still Takes 61% of US ATC Delay Minutes ??? Staffing Is Only 4%, But Seven Facilities Own 86% of It",
    excerpt:
      "FAA OPSNET 2024: 16.1M reportable delay minutes ??? weather 61%, volume 18%, runway 10%, other (incl. staffing) 8%, equipment 2%. Staffing alone is 623k minutes, and seven facilities hold 86% of that tail.",
    category: "Industry",
    themeId: "aviation-ops",
    imageUrl: "/images/industry-us-atc-delay-minutes-by-cause-2026-hero.png",
    imageAlt:
      "Dark navy radar-scope data visualization with cyan weather delay bars and amber staffing segments over a stylized US airspace silhouette",
    publishedAt: "2026-08-23T06:00:00Z",
    featured: true,
    visualization: "us-atc-delay-minutes-by-cause-2026",
    layout: "default",
    content: `When flights stack on the taxiway or hold for an EDCT, the Federal Aviation Administration's Operations Network (OPSNET) records a **reportable delay**: instrument-flight-rules traffic detained at least **15 minutes** by the ATC system. Those minutes are the National Airspace System's own stopwatch ??? not the passenger's gate-to-gate clock, and not the airline's irregular-operations ledger. In **2024**, OPSNET logged **16.07 million** delay minutes across **359,694** reportable delays. The cause stack is blunt: **weather took 61.4%** of the minutes. Volume, runway/taxiway, equipment, and the catch-all Other bucket split the rest. Staffing, coded only as a secondary cause under Other since mid-2022, was **622,669 minutes ??? 3.9% of the national total** ??? yet **seven facilities absorbed 86%** of that staffing slice.

The dashboard above treats delay minutes as a **share problem** and a **tail problem**. Toggle **Cause mix** for the decade stack and year donut, **Staffing tail** for facility bars, fill-rate scatter, and concentration curve, and **OPSNET vs BTS** for the taxonomy trap that makes ???weather is only 5% of delays??? headlines look true in passenger data while OPSNET says weather owns the majority of ATC minutes.

## Weather still owns the majority of ATC minutes

Primary OPSNET causes are mutually exclusive at the report level: **Weather**, **Volume**, **Equipment**, **Runway/taxiway**, and **Other**. Weather means adverse meteorology that cuts capacity ??? wind, rain, snow or ice, low ceilings and visibility, thunderstorms. In 2024 weather accounted for **9.86 million minutes** (**61.4%**). That is lower than the late-2010s weather share, when several years cleared **70%+** of minutes, but it remains the dominant primary cause every year in the 2015???2024 window except the pandemic trough.

Absolute weather minutes fell hard in 2020???2021 with traffic, then rebuilt: **7.6M (2022) ??? 8.7M (2023) ??? 9.9M (2024)**. The share story is slightly different from the level story. Weather's *percentage* of total minutes drifted down as equipment and Other grew faster off a small base, and as runway minutes jumped in 2024. Desks that only watch the weather share can miss that **weather minutes themselves rose more than 1.1 million year over year** even while the share eased from roughly 69% (2023) to 61% (2024).

## Volume, runway, and equipment are not interchangeable ???non-weather???

**Volume** is the purity test: delays may be coded volume only when the airport is in an optimum configuration and no impacting condition is reported. In 2024 volume was **2.92 million minutes (18.2%)** ??? the second-largest primary bucket. Volume is demand pressing against clean capacity, not a synonym for ???ATC staffing.???

**Runway/taxiway** delays ??? closures and configuration changes ??? reached **1.65 million minutes (10.3%)** in 2024, the highest runway minute total in the decade outside 2017's construction spike. **Equipment** remains small in share (**318k minutes, 2.0%**) but is no longer negligible in levels: equipment minutes roughly **quadrupled** from 2022 to 2024. Treating ???everything that is not weather??? as one residual hides that runway and equipment are **infrastructure and outage** stories, while volume is a **schedule-vs-capacity** story.

| Cause (2024) | Delay minutes | Share of minutes | Delays | Avg minutes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Weather | 9,861,692 | 61.4% | 193,056 | 51 |
| Volume | 2,924,101 | 18.2% | 98,323 | 29 |
| Runway / taxiway | 1,647,930 | 10.3% | 38,321 | 43 |
| Other (incl. staffing) | 1,313,470 | 8.2% | 24,174 | 54 |
| Equipment | 318,122 | 2.0% | 5,820 | 54 |
| **Total** | **16,065,315** | **100%** | **359,694** | **44** |

## Other is small nationally ??? until you open the staffing secondary code

**Other** covers airshows, VIP restrictions, military operations, and, since mid-2022, an explicit **staffing** secondary cause. Other was **8.2% of 2024 minutes** (**1.31 million**). Inside that bucket, staffing exploded: **22k minutes in 2022 ??? 90k in 2023 ??? 623k in 2024**. Staffing's share of Other minutes rose from **2% to 47%**. Average staffing delay lengthened from **23 to 49 minutes**.

Nationally, staffing is still only **~4% of all OPSNET minutes**. That is the correct headline if the question is ???what share of the NAS stopwatch is a staffing code???? It is the wrong headline if the question is ???where does the staffing problem live???? Concentration answers that.

## Seven facilities dominate the staffing minute tail

Of **622,669** staffing minutes in 2024, **86%** sat in seven facilities:

- **EWR** ??? 226,370 minutes (AFN fill rate 87%)
- **PHL** ??? 183,934 minutes (fill rate 130%)
- **ZNY** ??? 37,953 minutes (77%)
- **N90** ??? 36,744 minutes (74%)
- **AUS** ??? 18,096 minutes (80%)
- **ZJX** ??? 16,860 minutes (78%)
- **SFO** ??? 16,035 minutes (92%)

Newark and Philadelphia alone exceed **410,000 minutes** ??? roughly **two-thirds** of the national staffing total. The New York Center and New York TRACON add another **~75,000**. Jacksonville Center and Austin extend the map beyond the Northeast corridor; San Francisco closes the published top seven.

**PHL at 130% fill** is the scatter-plot outlier. National Academies analysis ties Philadelphia's staffing-coded delays to the deliberate transfer of Newark approach control duties ??? a safety-driven reallocation that shows up as delay minutes even when the receiving facility is overstaffed on paper. Fill rate and delay minutes are related, not identical; the dashboard scatter is built to keep that distinction visible.

## Core-30 geography already owns the delay map

Across **2022???2024**, Core 30 airports plus associated TRACONs and Centers accounted for about **92% of total OPSNET delay minutes** and **93% of Other minutes**. Nineteen facilities staffed at **85% or less** of target represented roughly **22% of operations** but about **39% of total delay minutes** and **45% of Other minutes**. The delay map is not a uniform fog over 500 towers. It is a **hub-and-center geometry** with a thin staffing secondary code that is even more skewed than the primary-cause map.

ARTCC identifiers in the staffing top seven ??? **ZNY** and **ZJX** ??? matter for the ???which centers dominate the tail???? question. Centers do not need to lead the *national* minute total to dominate the *staffing* tail; they appear when en-route sectors and adjacent TRACON/tower constraints couple. Towers and TRACONs (EWR, PHL, N90, AUS, SFO) still take most of the staffing minute mass in the published ranking.

## OPSNET weather is not BTS ???extreme weather???

Bureau of Transportation Statistics On-Time Performance uses a passenger taxonomy: **air carrier**, **late-arriving aircraft**, **National Aviation System (NAS)**, **extreme weather**, and **security**. Extreme weather is a **narrow** bucket ??? conditions that prevent flying. Most convective weather that slows the system without grounding it is coded **NAS**. Late-arriving aircraft then cascades prior causes into downstream turns.

That is why passenger-facing charts can show extreme weather near **~5%** of delay minutes while OPSNET shows weather near **~61%** of ATC minutes in the same year. The labels collide; the definitions do not. NAS in BTS absorbs volume, non-extreme weather, airport operations, and ATC effects that OPSNET splits across Weather, Volume, Runway, Equipment, and Other. Carrier and late-aircraft categories have **no OPSNET twin**. Comparing the two without a taxonomy bridge produces false ???weather is tiny / weather is everything??? debates.

## What the minute shares do ??? and do not ??? say

OPSNET minutes answer: *when the ATC system detains IFR traffic for 15+ minutes, what primary cause did the facility report, and how long did it last?* They do not answer passenger welfare directly, airline cost fully, or cancelation burden. They understate impacts shorter than 15 minutes. Staffing secondary coding begins mid-2022, so pre-2022 ???Other??? is not a clean staffing series. Average minutes rose inside Other even as counts swung ??? duration, not just incidence, moved.

For operations and policy desks, the actionable split is threefold. **First**, weather remains the majority of the NAS stopwatch; capacity and traffic-management investments that shrink weather impact still move the biggest slice. **Second**, runway and equipment are climbing in levels and should not be folded into a vague non-weather residual. **Third**, staffing is a **concentrated tail**: nationally small, locally decisive, with a Northeast corridor core and a handful of out-of-corridor facilities that punch above their operation share. The share question and the facility question are both true ??? they just describe different moments of the same OPSNET file.

Charted: Weather Still Takes 61% of US ATC Delay Minutes - Staffing Is Only 4%, But Seven Facilities Own 86% of It

Aug 23, 2026

FAA OPSNET 2024: 16.1M reportable delay minutes - weather 61%, volume 18%, runway 10%, other (incl. staffing) 8%, equipment 2%. Staffing alone is 623k minutes, and seven facilities hold 86% of that tail.

Loading interactive charts.

When flights stack on the taxiway or hold for an EDCT, the Federal Aviation Administration's Operations Network (OPSNET) records a reportable delay: instrument-flight-rules traffic detained at least 15 minutes by the ATC system. Those minutes are the National Airspace System's own stopwatch - not the passenger's gate-to-gate clock, and not the airline's irregular-operations ledger. In 2024, OPSNET logged 16.07 million delay minutes across 359,694 reportable delays. The cause stack is blunt: weather took 61.4% of the minutes. Volume, runway/taxiway, equipment, and the catch-all Other bucket split the rest. Staffing, coded only as a secondary cause under Other since mid-2022, was 622,669 minutes - 3.9% of the national total - yet seven facilities absorbed 86% of that staffing slice.

The dashboard above treats delay minutes as a share problem and a tail problem. Toggle Cause mix for the decade stack and year donut, Staffing tail for facility bars, fill-rate scatter, and concentration curve, and OPSNET vs BTS for the taxonomy trap that makes "weather is only 5% of delays" headlines look true in passenger data while OPSNET says weather owns the majority of ATC minutes.

Weather still owns the majority of ATC minutes

Primary OPSNET causes are mutually exclusive at the report level: Weather, Volume, Equipment, Runway/taxiway, and Other. Weather means adverse meteorology that cuts capacity - wind, rain, snow or ice, low ceilings and visibility, thunderstorms. In 2024 weather accounted for 9.86 million minutes (61.4%). That is lower than the late-2010s weather share, when several years cleared 70%+ of minutes, but it remains the dominant primary cause every year in the 2015-2024 window except the pandemic trough.

Absolute weather minutes fell hard in 2020-2021 with traffic, then rebuilt: 7.6M (2022)  8.7M (2023)  9.9M (2024). The share story is slightly different from the level story. Weather's percentage of total minutes drifted down as equipment and Other grew faster off a small base, and as runway minutes jumped in 2024. Desks that only watch the weather share can miss that weather minutes themselves rose more than 1.1 million year over year even while the share eased from roughly 69% (2023) to 61% (2024).

Volume, runway, and equipment are not interchangeable "non-weather"

Volume is the purity test: delays may be coded volume only when the airport is in an optimum configuration and no impacting condition is reported. In 2024 volume was 2.92 million minutes (18.2%) - the second-largest primary bucket. Volume is demand pressing against clean capacity, not a synonym for "ATC staffing."

Runway/taxiway delays - closures and configuration changes - reached 1.65 million minutes (10.3%) in 2024, the highest runway minute total in the decade outside 2017's construction spike. Equipment remains small in share (318k minutes, 2.0%) but is no longer negligible in levels: equipment minutes roughly quadrupled from 2022 to 2024. Treating "everything that is not weather" as one residual hides that runway and equipment are infrastructure and outage stories, while volume is a schedule-vs-capacity story.

Other is small nationally - until you open the staffing secondary code

Other covers airshows, VIP restrictions, military operations, and, since mid-2022, an explicit staffing secondary cause. Other was 8.2% of 2024 minutes (1.31 million). Inside that bucket, staffing exploded: 22k minutes in 2022  90k in 2023  623k in 2024. Staffing's share of Other minutes rose from 2% to 47%. Average staffing delay lengthened from 23 to 49 minutes.

Nationally, staffing is still only ~4% of all OPSNET minutes. That is the correct headline if the question is "what share of the NAS stopwatch is a staffing code?" It is the wrong headline if the question is "where does the staffing problem live?" Concentration answers that.

Seven facilities dominate the staffing minute tail

Charted: Weather Still Takes 61% of US ATC Delay Minutes - Staffing Is Only 4%, But Seven Facilities Own 86% of It

Aug 23, 2026

FAA OPSNET 2024: 16.1M reportable delay minutes - weather 61%, volume 18%, runway 10%, other (incl. staffing) 8%, equipment 2%. Staffing alone is 623k minutes, and seven facilities hold 86% of that tail.

Loading interactive charts.

When flights stack on the taxiway or hold for an EDCT, the Federal Aviation Administration's Operations Network (OPSNET) records a reportable delay: instrument-flight-rules traffic detained at least 15 minutes by the ATC system. Those minutes are the National Airspace System's own stopwatch - not the passenger's gate-to-gate clock, and not the airline's irregular-operations ledger. In 2024, OPSNET logged 16.07 million delay minutes across 359,694 reportable delays. The cause stack is blunt: weather took 61.4% of the minutes. Volume, runway/taxiway, equipment, and the catch-all Other bucket split the rest. Staffing, coded only as a secondary cause under Other since mid-2022, was 622,669 minutes - 3.9% of the national total - yet seven facilities absorbed 86% of that staffing slice.

The dashboard above treats delay minutes as a share problem and a tail problem. Toggle Cause mix for the decade stack and year donut, Staffing tail for facility bars, fill-rate scatter, and concentration curve, and OPSNET vs BTS for the taxonomy trap that makes "weather is only 5% of delays" headlines look true in passenger data while OPSNET says weather owns the majority of ATC minutes.

Weather still owns the majority of ATC minutes

Primary OPSNET causes are mutually exclusive at the report level: Weather, Volume, Equipment, Runway/taxiway, and Other. Weather means adverse meteorology that cuts capacity - wind, rain, snow or ice, low ceilings and visibility, thunderstorms. In 2024 weather accounted for 9.86 million minutes (61.4%). That is lower than the late-2010s weather share, when several years cleared 70%+ of minutes, but it remains the dominant primary cause every year in the 2015-2024 window except the pandemic trough.

Absolute weather minutes fell hard in 2020-2021 with traffic, then rebuilt: 7.6M (2022)  8.7M (2023)  9.9M (2024). The share story is slightly different from the level story. Weather's percentage of total minutes drifted down as equipment and Other grew faster off a small base, and as runway minutes jumped in 2024. Desks that only watch the weather share can miss that weather minutes themselves rose more than 1.1 million year over year even while the share eased from roughly 69% (2023) to 61% (2024).

Volume is the purity test: delays may be coded volume only when the airport is in an optimum configuration and no impacting condition is reported. In 2024 volume was 2.92 million minutes (18.2%) - the second-largest primary bucket. Volume is demand pressing against clean capacity, not a synonym for "ATC staffing."

Runway/taxiway delays - closures and configuration changes - reached 1.65 million minutes (10.3%) in 2024, the highest runway minute total in the decade outside 2017's construction spike. Equipment remains small in share (318k minutes, 2.0%) but is no longer negligible in levels: equipment minutes roughly quadrupled from 2022 to 2024. Treating "everything that is not weather" as one residual hides that runway and equipment are infrastructure and outage stories, while volume is a schedule-vs-capacity story.
